Earth heating faster: UN climate report says 2026 among 4 hottest years, El Nino rising
The WMO warned at COP31 that rising emissions and El Niño are driving exceptional global heat. The accelerating crisis threatens lives, livelihoods and food security worldwide.
Advertisement
The report said global temperatures were rising because the Earth was accumulating heat at an accelerating rate. (File photo)
The year 2026 is expected to be among the four warmest years on record, with the global average temperature between January and September reaching 1.47 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels, according to a World Meteorological Organization report cited by news agency Press Trust of India.
The average was higher than the full-year figures recorded in 2025 and 2023, and only slightly below 2024, the warmest year on record. It is likely to rise further by the end of 2026 because of the warming effect of El Nio, which has intensified since August and is expected to become the strongest on record by December.
The World Meteorological Organization released its State of the Climate Report on Friday, the opening day of the COP31 UN climate meeting in Antalya, Trkiye.
“The past four years have been the warmest in the 177-year observational record, and the heat in the oceans is breaking records for the tenth year in a row,” WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo said in a statement.
“The ongoing El Nio is forecast to be one of the strongest on record, and the heat it releases from the ocean will continue to fuel high temperatures and extreme weather into 2027,” she added.
The report said global temperatures were rising because the Earth was accumulating heat at an accelerating rate. Greenhouse gases were trapping unprecedented amounts of heat and disrupting the balance between energy received from the sun and energy released by the Earth. This imbalance reached its highest level since monitoring began.
According to the report cited by PTI, the concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere rose by 53 per cent, from around 278 parts per million in 1750 to about 426.8 parts per million in 2025. The global average concentration of methane increased by 167 per cent, from 729 parts per billion in 1750 to 1,948 parts per billion in 2025.
The oceans absorb 90 per cent of the excess heat, and 2026 is on course to become the tenth consecutive year of record ocean warmth, the report said.
The WMO also said extreme weather events had affected lives and livelihoods, weakened food security, deepened poverty and contributed to displacement in several regions. Preliminary estimates showed that heatwaves, drought and wildfires in Europe caused more than 30,000 excess deaths.
In India, an estimated 146.5 million people were exposed to extreme heat during a heatwave in April 2026, PTI reported, citing the WMO report.
“We have entered a new age of climate extremes. A supersized El Nio is colliding with a planet already superheated by manmade climate change. Climate records keep falling. The human costs keep rising,” UN Secretary-General AntÃ³nio Guterres said in a statement.
“And those least responsible are suffering first and worst. Leaders must get serious by cutting emissions faster, accelerating a just transition from fossil fuels and delivering the finance and protection vulnerable countries need,” he added.
advertisement
The WMO report said rising greenhouse gas levels, record ocean warmth and a strengthening El Nio were pushing global temperatures higher, while extreme weather continued to affect lives, livelihoods and food security across regions.

By: Mohamed Ibrahimrashid
Sunday November 8, 2026
Khudbaddii salaaddii Jimcaha ee 26-ka Jumada al-Awwal, 1448, xiiso dheeraad ah bay lahayd. Fadhiyadii jamaacada salaadda Jimcaha soo oogtay baa sidoo kale muujinayay dhag-raaricin. Siyaabaha khilaafaadka dawladnimo ee cusub loo xalliyo iyo dul-istaagga qoto-gaabnida ka jirta xirfadda aqooneed ee xallinta khilaafaadkaas bay jamaacadu dhegaysatay. Qoraalkan kooban waxaan ku soo koobayaa khudbaddii qaab falanqayn ah.
Khilaafaadka Soomaalida, oo marka miyiga la joogo garnaqsiga xeeladaha durugsan leh laga yaqaan, waxaa ku soo siyaaday khilaaf aan Soomaalida ku cusbayn, balse aqoonta loo leeyahay ay ka yartahay hal qarni oo qura. Waa khilaafka dawladnimada. Labada ugu muhiimsan ee khilaafaadka dawladdu yeelato waa midka ka dhex dhaca dawladda iyo shacabka, halka kan labaad uu yahay khilaafka ka dhex aloosma hay'adaha dawladda dhexdeeda.
Aayadda ugu dheer Qur'aanka, ee ku jirta aakhirka Suuratu al-Baqara, baa noqotay meel ay ku duugan tahay aqoonta khilaafaadka noocaas ah iyo sida loo wajaho. Jamaacada salaadda Jimcaha oogaysay ayaa khudbadda ugu horrayn ugu billowday su'aal isweydiin mudan: maxay ka hadli kartaa aayadda ugu dheer Qur'aanka? Cibaadada Alle oo keliya, jihaadka mise maqaasidda kale ee Islaamka? In la ogaado in aayaddu si gaar ah uga hadlayso khilaafaadka iyo sida loo xalliyo baa xiiso weyn lahayd. Waxaa lagu sheegay sida caddaaladda leh ee garta loo qaado iyo sida dadka loogu kala garniqo. Aayaddu waxay sidoo kale ka hadlaysaa dadka baahiyaha gaarka ah qaba ama aan awoodin inay xaqooda sheegtaan iyo sida loo kaalmaynayo.
Si aftahamo leh baa jamaacadu uga dhagaysteen imaamka ahmiyadda uu Qur'aanku siinayo ka hortagga khilaafaadka, isaga oo marka hore xoojinaya xurmada dadka ka shaqeeya xaqsooridda. Waxaa cajiib ah sida Eebbe Weyne u farayo in la xurmeeyo dadka qora dacwadaha iyo kuwa maragga fura, isaga oo u dammaanad dalbayo Allah ilaalin iyo xurmo dhidib adag ku taagan. Jamaacadu waxay dhegaysatay in ay jirto arrin muhiim ahi: xurmada madaxda garsoorka waa in la ilaaliyo, lagamana dhiirran karo in loo geysto hanjabaad, cabsi-gelin iyo xurmo-ka-qaadis, si aanu u dhicin isbarbaryaac bulsho oo kala dambaynta wiiqa.
Meel aayaddu waxay marqaatiyada ku faraysaa inaanay diidin haddii loo yeero. Isla aayadda dhammaadkeeda, marqaatiyadii loo yeeray ee laga dalbaday inay gutaan waajibaadkooda, Alle wuxuu faray in aan wax dhib iyo shiddo loo gaysan. Taas macnaheedu waa in awoodaha garsoorka, iyo cid kasta oo qayb ka noqonaysa xallinta khilaafaadka, ay mudan yihiin in la xurmeeyo oo la ilaaliyo.
Khudbad noocan ahi waxay ku soo aadaysaa xilli dalkeennu ku jiro xaalad siyaasadeed oo qar ku socota. In laga maqlo minaaradaha baaca dheer ee ka qotoma deris kasta agtiisa, waa horumar xoojinaya suuragalnimada baaq nabadeed, helidda waanooyinka midnimada qaranka ku aaddan iyo xoojinta walaalnimada iyo Soomaalinimada.
Waxay kaloo khudbadaha noocan ahi abuuraan aqoon iyo wacyi la garab dhigayo dhaqanka qalalaasaha ee dalkeennu soo maray. Halka loo noqonayo ee ummaddu ku kalsoonaan karto baa ah in la fahmo xurmada ay mudan tahay.

On a blistering summer day in 1945, Nat King Cole’s holiday classic was written.
James Tormé, son of the song’s writer Mel Tormé, told NPR in a 2017 interview what inspired his father and his writing partner Bob Wells to write one of the most beloved Christmas songs of all time:
“It was a very hot, sort of an oppressive summer,” Tormé explained. “And my father went to the house of his then-writing partner, a guy called Bob Wells. And Wells was nowhere to be seen. But there was a spiral pad at the piano. There were four lines sort of scribbled down on it in pencil – ‘chestnuts roasting on an open fire, Jack Frost nipping at your nose, yuletide carols being sung by a choir, and folks dressed up like Eskimos.’”
Tormé continued, “When Bob Wells eventually appeared he said, you know, ‘Mel, I have tried everything to cool down. I’ve been in my pool. I had a cold drink. I’ve taken a cold shower. I’m nothing but hot. And I thought that maybe, you know, if I could just write down a few lines of wintery verse I could psychologically get an edge over this heat.’”
“So my dad sort of looked at Bob, looked back down at the spiral pad, and then looked back at Wells and said, ‘I think there’s something here,’” Tormé recalled. “And about 45 minutes later – no more than that – the song was born.”
The Nat King Cole Trio recorded the song the next year in 1946, and 80 years later the song is still a top pick for most people’s Christmas playlists. It peaked in the 2013-2014 winter season when it reached the #2 spot on the Holiday Streaming Songs chart, and it’s far and away the singer’s most streamed song on Spotify at over 757 million listens.
In 2017, Billboard ranked the song #3 on their list of best Christmas songs, praising its peaceful string-and-piano sound and its cozy, warm vibes. “It’s no wonder that the song is generically titled ‘The Christmas Song,’” the publication wrote, “because it perfectly encapsulates the best of Christmas music with its sense of homey familiarity.”
Related: Nat King Cole’s 1955 Hit, Originally Sung in French, Ranked Best Song for Your Autumn Playlist.
It was hard to imagine how popular the song would be at the time. As Tormé told NPR, when Mel Tormé and Bob Wells tried to sell it to Burke/Van Heusen publishing, they were declined.
“Nobody would ever want a song like this, that’s only really going to be popular one day of the year,” Tormé said. “So they, a little bit dejected, took the song the same afternoon to the house of a guy called Nat Cole.”
Tormé recalled, “[Nat] said, ‘Stop everything. That’s my song.’”

A computer model of a Bose-Einstein condensate,(NASA/NIST)
Even the seemingly empty vacuum of space isn't completely cold.
The Universe was born some 13.8 billion years ago in a state so hot and dense that the leftover radiation still permeates every one of its nooks and crannies.
The average background temperature of space hovers around 2.7 kelvins – that's -270.45 degrees Celsius, or -454.81 Fahrenheit.
Now, scientists have made something with an equivalent temperature 280 billion times lower – shattering the previous record in humanity's quest to get as close as possible to absolute zero.
Aboard China's Tiangong space station in Earth orbit, physicists have achieved a record equivalent temperature of just 9.7 picokelvins – or 0.0000000000097 kelvins – "which is, to our knowledge, the lowest equivalent temperature ever measured," the researchers write in a paper published in Science.
Absolute zero – or zero kelvins – is the theoretical lower limit temperature can reach in the Universe. At that point, thermal energy physically cannot plunge any lower. It's like the speed of light – a fundamental limit that the laws of physics simply cannot cross.
Unlike the speed of light, however, absolute zero is impossible to reach. The closer scientists get, the harder it becomes to remove the remaining thermal energy, until reaching the limit would require a cooling process that could never be completed.
But that hasn't stopped physicists from trying – and the closer they get, the weirder matter begins to behave.
One of the best examples is the Bose-Einstein condensate, an exotic state of matter that forms when certain atoms are cooled to temperatures just fractions of a degree above absolute zero.
At these extremes, the atoms begin to behave collectively, their individual quantum states merging into a single, coherent whole. They stop acting as a collection of separate particles and instead function almost like one enormous quantum object.
Because quantum effects are usually most apparent on the atomic scale, Bose-Einstein condensates allow scientists to study quantum behavior on a much larger scale, rather than trying to observe it in individual atoms.
They can also be used to make extraordinarily sensitive measurements of the physical world, potentially helping scientists probe some of the fundamental laws governing the Universe.
But making Bose-Einstein condensates isn't easy, and here on Earth, the process comes up against an inescapable limit – gravity, which makes it increasingly difficult to cool atoms to such extremes.
So the researchers took their experiment somewhere gravity would pose much less of a problem: space.
They are not the first. NASA created the first Bose-Einstein condensate in orbit aboard the International Space Station in 2018, cooling a cloud of rubidium atoms to 100 nanokelvins.
Since then, others have pushed that envelope even further, with the previous record of 38 picokelvins achieved during a free-fall experiment in Germany's Bremen Drop Tower, described in a 2021 paper.
The new experiment, led by physicists Xiaoji Zhou and Xuzong Chen of Peking University, and Weibiao Chen of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, took advantage of the prolonged microgravity environment to push the limits of cooling even further.
As many others have before them, the researchers began with a cloud of rubidium-87 atoms – an isotope of the element particularly well suited to laser cooling and the creation of Bose-Einstein condensates.
They used lasers to cool the atoms, confined in an optical trap in an apparatus called the Cold Atom Physics Rack.
Then, they applied a technique called evaporative cooling, in which the most energetic atoms are allowed to escape, leaving the remaining atoms with less energy. It's like your coffee growing cold as its most energetic molecules escape as vapor.
Here, though, gravity once again decided to be a problem. On Earth, gravity can help this process by pulling the escaping atoms away from the trap. In orbit, where everything is in continuous free fall, that assistance is missing.
So, having gone to space to rid themselves of gravity, the researchers had to find a way to recreate gravity.
They did this by applying a magnetic field gradient that mimicked gravity's effect on the atoms, allowing the most energetic ones to escape more efficiently.
At this point, the experiment contained a Bose-Einstein condensate of around 20,000 rubidium atoms, cooled to a temperature of just 3.1 nanokelvins.
But the researchers weren't done.
They transferred the condensate into a second, wider trap made of laser light, then gradually weakened the trap, allowing the cloud of atoms to spread out and reducing the energy it would release as it expanded.
Finally, they switched off the trap altogether and watched the cloud disperse.
It expanded so slowly that the researchers could still detect the atoms seven seconds after their release.
By measuring how quickly the cloud spread, the team calculated its equivalent temperature: a record-breaking 9.7 picokelvins.
This isn't quite the same as the conventional temperature. Equivalent temperature instead describes the energy associated with the cloud's expansion. It's seeing how slowly the atoms are moving, using that motion to determine how much energy they have, and expressing that energy in kelvins.
And for scientists hoping to use these clouds of atoms to make extraordinarily precise measurements, that distinction is important. The more slowly the atoms disperse, the longer they can be observed and manipulated – and the more sensitive those measurements can become.
The point isn't just about setting temperature records. The result has some really cool implications for future research, too.
One particularly promising application is atom interferometry, which exploits the wave-like properties of atoms to measure extraordinarily small changes in their environment.
With more time to observe the atoms, scientists could build more sensitive instruments for testing fundamental physics, including the equivalence principle – the idea that gravity affects all objects equally, regardless of their mass or composition.
The ability to produce such ultracold quantum gases in space could also allow researchers to explore exotic states of matter that are difficult to study in laboratories on Earth.
"This all-optical ultracold platform … meets the exacting requirements for quantum simulation and precision metrology in future space missions, thus positioning it to advance two primary scientific frontiers," the researchers write.

Source: Xinhua
Editor: huaxia

BEIJING, Nov. 9 (Xinhua) -- Beijing will activate an orange alert for heavy air pollution starting from Nov. 11, the Beijing Municipal Ecology and Environment Bureau said on Monday.
According to air quality forecasts, unfavorable meteorological conditions will lead to a regional air pollution episode affecting the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region and surrounding areas in north China.
From Nov. 11 to Nov. 14, Beijing's air quality is expected to reach moderate pollution levels, with some areas and periods reaching severe pollution levels.
In response, the city will activate the orange alert -- the second-highest level in China's four-tier emergency response system. Residents are advised to take appropriate health precautions. ■

Weather conditions in the UK are creating the “perfect recipe” for fog, the Met Office has said, as it issued a warning over difficult travel conditions.
A yellow weather warning forecasting fog across large parts of the country runs from 6pm on Sunday until 11am on Monday, with the potential for disruption to flights.
The warning area, which stretches from York to Bath and covers most of the South East and eastern England, will likely see the densest fog, but low-lying cloud will still affect other areas.
The warning covers the West Midlands, Staffordshire, Shropshire and Mid Wales.
Niamh Murray, Met Office operational meteorologist, said: “There is still going to be patchy fog elsewhere, just not quite as dense or as impactful.
“Parts of the West Country could still see fog, Northern Ireland, really anywhere across much of the UK, even into the central belt of Scotland.”
Ms Murray said current weather conditions are the “perfect recipe” for fog.
“With autumn and winter and getting fog during this time of year, we get much longer nights, and that allows temperatures to sort of fall away,” she told the Press Association.
“We get a longer period of cooling and also the temperatures are much lower, so they’re much closer to the temperature that we need for the air to become saturated and therefore form fog.
“Another thing that we need to form fog is quite light winds, not absolutely no winds.
“We just have the perfect recipe at the moment: light winds, clear skies, long nights, to allow that fog to develop. And particularly if we see the negative numbers, it can quite stubborn to clear the next day.”
Fog may be particularly stubborn overnight into Monday in rural parts of the Midlands, Wales and East Anglia, where temperatures will drop near to freezing, with air frost possible.
Visibility could be down to 50 metres or less in some places, the Met Office warned, with delays to bus and train services possible and a chance of delays or cancellations to flights.
From Tuesday to Thursday, some “pretty welcome” rain is forecast, Ms Murray said.
“Most places are likely to see 10 to 20mm and there is a chance that we could see some places seeing 30mm,” she said.
“But across the South West, where severe drought has been declared and is still enforced by the Environment Agency, there is a chance that we might see some very slow-moving rain, and you could see potentially accumulations up to 50 to 70 mm.”
